account: A 34-year-old right-handed woman took part in a single-case proof of concept at the University of Messina and IRCCS Centro Neurolesi Bonino-Pulejo. She has right hemiparesis, global aphasia and dysarthria from a massive left-hemisphere hemorrhage at age 19. A compact convolutional neural network in CapisciAMe used recordings from her and 69 other Italian speakers with dysarthria. She supplied 1,120 utterances of 13 target words. The methods describe 21,947 training and 1,162 validation utterances, with her November 2022 recordings held out for testing. The tailored recognizer identified 680 of 936 test utterances (72.65%). The developers first posted the study as a JMIR preprint on 7 August 2025, with a listener mean of 56.2%. The case report appeared in Frontiers in Rehabilitation Sciences on 3 June 2026. In it, twelve rehabilitation professionals averaged 56.75% on a separate open-response listening task with 26 recordings each. The authors state that the items heard by listeners were not logged, so the recognizer and the listeners cannot be compared item by item. No real-world communication use is documented.

segment: Adults with post-stroke aphasia and dysarthria
summary: CapisciAMe, a speech recognizer tailored to a woman with aphasia and dysarthria, identified 72.65% of 936 recorded test words; twelve professional listeners averaged 56.75% on a separate task.
system: CapisciAMe speaker-dependent ASR (compact convolutional neural network, cnn-trad-fpool3) in a voice-input voice-output communication aid
taxonomy_note: The recognizer is a communication aid for a woman with dysarthria, but only a laboratory accuracy result is documented.
title: CapisciAMe recognizes recorded words from a woman with aphasia and dysarthria in a laboratory study
unrated_because: The authors report recognition accuracy on recorded test words and document no use of the recognizer in the woman's daily communication.
